column2: The null hypothesis in a significance test is a claim of:
column3: No difference or no change from a specified value for the population parameter
column4: A large and meaningful difference from a specified value for the population parameter
column5: No variability or no spread in the values observed within the collected sample data
column6: A statistically significant result that supports what the research team hoped to find

column2: The alternative hypothesis is the claim that:
column3: Researchers hope to find evidence for, based on the data they have collected
column4: Is assumed to be true at the start and maintained unless evidence says otherwise
column5: Describes what would happen if no effect or no difference exists in the population
column6: Must always be stated after the data have been collected and the results are known

column2: The null hypothesis for a test about a population proportion always takes the form:
column3: H0: p = p0, where p0 is the hypothesized value of the population proportion
column4: H0: p-hat = p0, where p0 is the hypothesized value of the sample proportion
column5: H0: p > p0, where p0 is the hypothesized value of the population proportion
column6: H0: p ≠ p0, where p0 is the hypothesized value of the population proportion

column2: The null hypothesis always contains:
column3: An equality sign, such as p equals some specified numerical value
column4: A strict inequality sign, such as less than, greater than, or not equal to
column5: A sample statistic like p-hat rather than a population parameter like p
column6: A reference to the specific data values that were observed in the sample

column2: The alternative hypothesis always contains:
column3: A strict inequality, such as less than, greater than, or not equal to
column4: An equality sign, such as p equals some specified numerical value
column5: A sample statistic like p-hat rather than a population parameter like p
column6: The exact same claim that appears in the corresponding null hypothesis

column2: An alternative hypothesis of the form Ha: p > p0 is called:
column3: One-sided, because only evidence above the null value would support the claim
column4: Two-sided, because evidence on either side of the null value would support the claim
column5: One-sided, because only evidence below the null value would support the claim
column6: Undirected, because the direction of the difference has not been specified yet

column2: An alternative hypothesis of the form Ha: p ≠ p0 is called:
column3: Two-sided, because evidence on either side of the null value would support the claim
column4: One-sided, because only evidence above the null value would support the claim
column5: One-sided, because only evidence below the null value would support the claim
column6: Balanced, because the null and alternative carry equal weight in the analysis

column2: When should the alternative hypothesis be determined?
column3: Before the data are collected, based on the research question being investigated
column4: After the data are collected, based on what the observed results look like
column5: During the data analysis, once the direction of the result becomes clear
column6: At any point in the study, since the timing of the decision does not matter

column2: Hypotheses should be written using:
column3: Population parameters like p, because hypotheses are claims about the population
column4: Sample statistics like p-hat, because hypotheses are claims about the sample data
column5: Either parameters or statistics, since both are acceptable in hypothesis notation
column6: Descriptive words only, because symbolic notation is not required on the AP exam

column2: A student writes 'H0: p-hat = 0.60' in their hypothesis statement. This is:
column3: Incorrect — hypotheses must use the population parameter p, not the sample statistic p-hat
column4: Correct — p-hat is the appropriate symbol to use when stating any hypothesis about a proportion
column5: Incorrect — the null hypothesis should use p-hat but the value should always be set to zero
column6: Correct — but only when the sample size is large enough to satisfy the conditions for inference

column2: When defining the parameter p in your hypotheses, you should describe it as:
column3: The proportion of all members of the population who have the characteristic of interest
column4: The proportion of members in the sample who were observed to have the characteristic
column5: The number of individuals in the sample who were counted as having the characteristic
column6: The difference between the observed and expected values of the sample proportion

column2: A researcher wants to know if a proportion is greater than 0.30. The correct alternative is:
column3: Ha: p > 0.30, because the researcher specifically suspects the proportion is above 0.30
column4: Ha: p ≠ 0.30, because the researcher is looking for any difference from 0.30 at all
column5: Ha: p < 0.30, because the researcher needs to test the opposite direction as well
column6: Ha: p = 0.30, because the alternative should match the value the researcher suspects

column2: A researcher wants to know if a proportion 'differs from' 0.50. The correct alternative is:
column3: Ha: p ≠ 0.50, because 'differs from' does not specify a particular direction
column4: Ha: p > 0.50, because 'differs from' implies the proportion should be larger
column5: Ha: p < 0.50, because 'differs from' implies the proportion should be smaller
column6: Ha: p = 0.50, because the word 'differs' means the parameter equals the given value

column2: A researcher suspects the proportion is less than a claimed value. The correct alternative is:
column3: Ha: p < p0, because the research question specifically suggests a direction below the claim
column4: Ha: p > p0, because the research question specifically suggests a direction above the claim
column5: Ha: p ≠ p0, because any time a researcher has a suspicion the test should be two-sided
column6: Ha: p = p0, because the alternative must match the value from the original stated claim

column2: Until we have convincing evidence otherwise, we assume that:
column3: The null hypothesis is true — it is the default position at the start of any significance test
column4: The alternative hypothesis is true — it is what the researcher expects to find in the data
column5: Both hypotheses are equally likely to be true at the beginning of the significance testing
column6: Neither hypothesis is true — we remain completely neutral until the analysis is finished

column2: The appropriate significance test procedure for testing a single population proportion is:
column3: A one-sample z-test for a population proportion, using the normal sampling distribution
column4: A two-sample z-test for a difference in proportions, using paired sample methodology
column5: A one-sample t-test for a population proportion, using the t sampling distribution
column6: A chi-square goodness-of-fit test for a proportion, using the chi-square distribution

column2: The one-sample z-test is used specifically when the goal is to:
column3: Test a claim about the proportion of successes in a single population using sample data
column4: Estimate the proportion of successes in a population by constructing a confidence interval
column5: Compare the proportions of successes between two separate and independent populations
column6: Test a claim about the mean of a population when the standard deviation is unknown

column2: The one-sample z-test for a proportion and the one-sample z-interval for a proportion:
column3: Are different procedures — one performs a significance test and the other constructs an interval
column4: Are the exact same procedure with two different names for the same statistical analysis
column5: Cannot both be applied to the same data set because their conditions are incompatible
column6: Always produce the same numerical conclusion when applied to the same set of sample data

column2: The first condition to check before performing a one-sample z-test for a proportion is:
column3: The data were collected using a random sample from the population of interest
column4: The sample size is at least 30 observations to ensure normality of the distribution
column5: The population proportion is known so that it can be compared to the sample result
column6: The standard deviation of the population is given somewhere in the problem statement

column2: The 10% condition requires that when sampling without replacement:
column3: The sample size n is no more than 10% of the population size N to ensure independence
column4: The population size N is no more than 10% of the sample size n to ensure accuracy
column5: At least 10% of the population must be included in the sample for sufficient precision
column6: The margin of error must be less than 10% to make the confidence interval meaningful

column2: If the population size is not given in the problem, the 10% condition should be handled by:
column3: Stating that it is reasonable to assume the population is at least 10 times the sample size
column4: Skipping the condition entirely because it cannot be checked without the population size
column5: Concluding that the condition is automatically not met when the population size is unknown
column6: Using the sample size as an estimate of the population size to complete the calculation

column2: The Large Counts condition for a one-sample z-test requires:
column3: np0 ≥ 10 and n(1 - p0) ≥ 10, where p0 is the proportion from the null hypothesis
column4: n*p-hat ≥ 10 and n*(1 - p-hat) ≥ 10, where p-hat is the observed sample proportion
column5: np0 ≥ 30 and n(1 - p0) ≥ 30, where p0 is the proportion from the null hypothesis
column6: n*p-hat ≥ 30 and n*(1 - p-hat) ≥ 30, where p-hat is the observed sample proportion

column2: The Large Counts condition for a significance test uses p0 instead of p-hat because:
column3: In a significance test we assume the null hypothesis is true, so we use its value of p0
column4: In a significance test p-hat is not available until after the conditions have been checked
column5: The value of p0 is always larger than p-hat, which makes the condition easier to satisfy
column6: Using p-hat would require knowing the population size, which is often not given in problems

column2: The Large Counts condition for a confidence interval uses p-hat, but for a significance test it uses p0. The reason for this difference is:
column3: A CI has no hypothesized value to assume, but a test assumes the null hypothesis is true
column4: A CI always has a larger sample size, which changes which value is appropriate to use
column5: A test requires p-hat for the calculation while a CI requires p0 for the same calculation
column6: There is actually no difference — both procedures should always use the same value of p-hat

column2: The Large Counts condition ensures that:
column3: The sampling distribution of p-hat is approximately normal, so the z-test is appropriate
column4: The sample is representative of the population, so the results can be generalized to all
column5: The sample was collected randomly, so the observations are independent of each other
column6: The population proportion is close to 0.50, so the test will have sufficient statistical power

column2: For a test with H0: p = 0.70 and n = 50, the Large Counts check is:
column3: 50(0.70) = 35 ≥ 10 and 50(0.30) = 15 ≥ 10, so the condition is satisfied
column4: 50(0.70) = 35 ≥ 30 and 50(0.30) = 15 ≥ 30, so the condition is not satisfied
column5: 50(0.50) = 25 ≥ 10 and 50(0.50) = 25 ≥ 10, so the condition is satisfied
column6: 50(0.30) = 15 ≥ 10 and 50(0.70) = 35 ≥ 10, so the condition is satisfied

column2: For a test with H0: p = 0.05 and n = 80, the Large Counts condition:
column3: Is not satisfied, because np0 = 80(0.05) = 4, which is less than the required value of 10
column4: Is satisfied, because n(1 - p0) = 80(0.95) = 76, which exceeds the required value of 10
column5: Is satisfied, because the sample size of 80 is large enough by itself to meet the condition
column6: Is not satisfied, because n(1 - p0) = 80(0.95) = 76, which exceeds the required value of 10

column2: All three conditions for a one-sample z-test must be checked because:
column3: Each condition ensures a different aspect of the test is valid — randomness, independence, shape
column4: Checking only one condition is sufficient, but the AP exam requires writing all three out
column5: The conditions are redundant with each other, but convention requires verifying each one
column6: Only the Large Counts condition actually matters; the other two are merely suggested steps

column2: If the conditions for a one-sample z-test are not all satisfied, then:
column3: We should not proceed with the test because the results may not be statistically valid
column4: We can still proceed with the test but must report a lower confidence level in the results
column5: We should switch to a two-sample z-test, which has less restrictive conditions to check
column6: We should increase the significance level to compensate for the unmet condition in the test

column2: A one-sided alternative hypothesis should be used when:
column3: The research question asks specifically whether the proportion is above or below a value
column4: The researcher is unsure whether the proportion is above or below the hypothesized value
column5: The sample size is too small to support a two-sided alternative hypothesis for the test
column6: The null hypothesis value is exactly 0.50 and the sampling distribution is symmetric

column2: A two-sided alternative hypothesis should be used when:
column3: The research question asks whether the proportion differs from a value in either direction
column4: The researcher has strong reason to believe the proportion is specifically above the value
column5: The researcher has strong reason to believe the proportion is specifically below the value
column6: The sample data show a result in one direction that the researcher wants to confirm

column2: Which of the following would be a correctly defined parameter for a hypothesis test?
column3: p = the proportion of all registered voters in the state who would support the new policy
column4: p = the proportion of the 200 surveyed voters who said they support the new policy

column6: p-hat = the number of surveyed voters who responded yes to the question about the policy

column2: Using 'would say' instead of 'said' when defining a parameter matters because:
column3: 'Would say' refers to the entire population; 'said' refers only to the people actually sampled
column4: 'Would say' is grammatically correct; 'said' is grammatically incorrect in statistics notation
column5: 'Would say' indicates a larger sample size; 'said' indicates a smaller sample size was used
column6: 'Would say' is required only on the AP exam; 'said' is acceptable in all other contexts

column2: The three conditions for a one-sample z-test for a proportion are:
column3: Random sample, 10% condition (n ≤ 10% of N), and Large Counts (np0 ≥ 10 and n(1-p0) ≥ 10)
column4: Random sample, sample size at least 30, and Large Counts (np-hat ≥ 10 and n(1-p-hat) ≥ 10)
column5: Normal population, 10% condition (n ≤ 10% of N), and known population standard deviation
column6: Random sample, equal sample sizes in both groups, and Large Counts (np0 ≥ 5 and n(1-p0) ≥ 5)

column2: After verifying that all conditions for a one-sample z-test are met, the next step is to:
column3: Proceed to calculations — compute the test statistic and find the p-value for the test
column4: Restate the hypotheses using different notation before moving on to the calculations
column5: Collect additional data to further verify that the conditions are satisfied for the test
column6: Choose whether to use a one-sided or two-sided alternative based on the observed results
